title: Some Procrustes-type Problems
html:
Procrustes in the Greek mythology fits his guests to his bed. The mathematical problem after his name has a similar flavour. Suppose we have two set of vectors XXX, YYY, where columns represent the vectors, and we want to find a linear transform QQQ that takes XXX to YYY, QX=YQX = YQX=Y meaning we assume the column-to-column correspondence. If there is no constraint on what kind of transform we would like to have, then the answer can be Q=YX†Q = YX^{\dagger}Q=YX† where X†=XT(XXT)−1X^{\dagger} = X^{T}(XX^{T})^{-1}X†=XT(XXT)−1 assuming XXTXX^{T}XXT invertible. The question is more instereting when we constrain QQQ to be a rotation with possible reflection (i.e. orthonormal) QTQ=IQ^{T}Q = IQTQ=I which is of practical interests. Now its clear we don't always have QX=YQX=YQX=Y, so it's natural to ask for the solution of arg⁡min⁡QTQ=I∥QX−Y∥F2\arg\min_{Q^TQ=I} \|QX-Y\|_{F}^2argminQTQ=I​∥QX−Y∥F2​ where ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F}∥⋅∥F​ denotes the Frobenius norm. In other words, we want the transformed vectors QXQXQX to be closest to YYY in a least square sense. Below the fold we will describe two ways to solve this problem with closed form solution.

Two approaches to the orthonormal Procrustes Problem

The first way is through standard constrained optimization approach. We consider the Lagrangian L(Q,Λ)=∥QX−Y∥F2+∑i,jΛ⊙(QTQ−I)L(Q, \Lambda) = \|QX-Y\|_{F}^2 + \sum_{i,j} \Lambda \odot (Q^TQ - I)L(Q,Λ)=∥QX−Y∥F2​+∑i,j​Λ⊙(QTQ−I) where ⊙\odot⊙ denotes the entries-wise multiplication of matrices, sometimes called Hardamard product; the summation is over all indices. To find a critical point of LLL and hence the minimum of the convex objective, we would need to differentiate L(Q,Λ)L(Q,\Lambda)L(Q,Λ) with respect to entries of QQQ. To make our life easier, we will need to simplify the expression, by using the following identites for AAA, BBB of size m×nm\times nm×n: ∥A∥F2=tr(ATA)tr(ATB)=tr(BAT)=∑i,jA⊙B∂∂Xijtr(XTAX)=((AT+A)X)ij∂∂Xijtr(AX)=Aji\begin{aligned} \|A\|_{F}^2 = \text{tr}(A^{T}A) \\ \text{tr}(A^TB) = \text{tr}(BA^T) = \sum_{i,j} A \odot B \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial X_{ij}}\text{tr}(X^TAX) = ((A^T + A)X)_{ij} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial X_{ij}}\text{tr}(AX) = A_{ji} \end{aligned}∥A∥F2​=tr(ATA)tr(ATB)=tr(BAT)=i,j∑​A⊙B∂Xij​∂​tr(XTAX)=((AT+A)X)ij​∂Xij​∂​tr(AX)=Aji​​ First, we write L(Q,Λ)=tr(QXXTQT)−2tr(XYTQ)+tr(YTY)+tr(ΛT(QTQ−I)).L(Q,\Lambda) = \text{tr}(QXX^TQ^T) - 2\text{tr}(XY^TQ) + \text{tr}(Y^TY) + \text{tr}(\Lambda^T(Q^TQ-I)).L(Q,Λ)=tr(QXXTQT)−2tr(XYTQ)+tr(YTY)+tr(ΛT(QTQ−I)). Differentiate in QQQ gives ∂L∂Q=2QXXT−2YXT+Q(ΛT+Λ)\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q} = 2QXX^T - 2YX^T + Q(\Lambda^T + \Lambda)∂Q∂L​=2QXXT−2YXT+Q(ΛT+Λ) Setting this to zero, we have (ΛT+Λ)/2+XXT=QTYXT(\Lambda^T + \Lambda)/2 + XX^T = Q^TYX^T(ΛT+Λ)/2+XXT=QTYXT Now here is the crux. This means QTXYTQ^TXY^TQTXYT must be symmetric QTYXT=XYTQQ^TYX^T = XY^TQQTYXT=XYTQ Multiplying both sides by QQQ, we get YXT=QXYTQYX^T = QXY^TQYXT=QXYTQ Squaring both sides, YXTXYT=QXYTYXTQTYX^TXY^T = QXY^TYX^TQ^TYXTXYT=QXYTYXTQT Suppose the eigen decopositions are YXTXYT=VDVT,XYTYXT=UDUTYX^TXY^T = VDV^T, XY^TYX^T = UDU^TYXTXYT=VDVT,XYTYXT=UDUT since we know they have the same eigenvalues, we must have V=QUV = QUV=QU or Q=VUTQ = VU^TQ=VUT. We can compute the matrices UUU and VVV by computing the singular value decomposition of XYTXY^TXYT XYT=UΣVTXY^T = U\Sigma V^TXYT=UΣVT In the second approach we will effectively prove Q=UVTQ = UV^TQ=UVT is the solution. We write ∥QX−Y∥F2=∥QX∥F2−2tr(XYTQ)+∥Y∥F2\|QX-Y\|_{F}^2 = \|QX\|_{F}^2 - 2\text{tr}(XY^TQ) + \|Y\|_{F}^2∥QX−Y∥F2​=∥QX∥F2​−2tr(XYTQ)+∥Y∥F2​ The last term has nothing to do with QQQ, so can be safely ignored. Now we invoke a lemma.

Lemma 1 If QQQ is an orthonormal matrix, then ∥QX∥F2=∥X∥F2\|QX\|_{F}^2 = \|X\|_{F}^2∥QX∥F2​=∥X∥F2​ for any matrix XXX.

Hence in fact the first term does not matter as well. We now want to maximize tr(XYTQ)\text{tr}(XY^TQ)tr(XYTQ) We proceed by taking the singluar value decomposition of XYT=UΣVTXY^T= U\Sigma V^TXYT=UΣVT, to get tr(XYTQ)=tr(UΣVTQ)=tr(ΣVTQU)\begin{aligned} \text{tr}(XY^TQ) &= \text{tr}(U\Sigma V^TQ) \\ &= \text{tr}(\Sigma V^TQU) \end{aligned}tr(XYTQ)​=tr(UΣVTQ)=tr(ΣVTQU)​ Note that Σ\SigmaΣ is diagonal and recall that they are all positive. So we are instereted in maximizing the diagonal entries of VTQUV^TQUVTQU.

Lemma 2 If u,vu, vu,v are unit vectors, then ⟨u,v⟩\langle u, v\rangle⟨u,v⟩ is at most 111.

Viewing VTQV^TQVTQ together, the first diagonal entry in the dot product between the fisrt row of VTQV^TQVTQ and the first column of UUU, and it is at most 111. It is then easy to see that the diagonal entries are maximized when VTQU=IV^TQU = IVTQU=I We again arrive at the solution Q=VUTQ = VU^TQ=VUT.

Relation to As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation

In ARAP, an important subproblem to solve is the following arg⁡min⁡QTQ=I∥∇f−Q∥F2   (1)\arg\min_{Q^TQ = I} \|\nabla f - Q\|_F^2 \,\,\,(1)argminQTQ=I​∥∇f−Q∥F2​(1) where fff is a mapping between two triangulated surfaes and we usually assume det⁡∇f\det \nabla fdet∇f to be positive. Since locally on a triangle, ∇f\nabla f∇f maps edges to edges linearly. In the language of Procrustes problem, we are actually looking for arg⁡min⁡QTQ=I∥YX−1−Q∥F2\arg\min_{Q^TQ = I} \|YX^{-1}- Q\|_F^2argminQTQ=I​∥YX−1−Q∥F2​ where we assume X,YX, YX,Y are square and invertible. It is curious to note that this problem is not equivalent to the original Procrustes problem arg⁡min⁡QTQ=I∥QX−Y∥F2   (2)\arg\min_{Q^TQ=I} \|QX-Y\|_{F}^2 \,\,\,(2)argminQTQ=I​∥QX−Y∥F2​(2) which is actually equivalent to arg⁡min⁡QTQ=I∥YXT−Q∥F2\arg\min_{Q^TQ=I} \|YX^T-Q\|_{F}^2argminQTQ=I​∥YXT−Q∥F2​ It turns out we can relate Problem (1) to Problem (2) by reweighing the quadratic energy column-wisely with respect to the geometry of the domain vectors, namely the cotangent weight. We refer to a previous post for details on that formulation.

A more general problem

Now we focus on Problem (1). Suppose we allow QQQ to be different from a orthonormal a bit. To be precise, we set bounds to the singular values σ1,σ2\sigma_1, \sigma_2σ1​,σ2​ of QQQ, namely k≤σ2<σ1≤Kk \leq \sigma_2 < \sigma_1 \leq Kk≤σ2​<σ1​≤K We again ask what would be the best QQQ that maps XXX to YYY in a least square sense. It's tempting to suggest that the answer is Q=UΣ∗VTQ = U \Sigma^{*}V^TQ=UΣ∗VT, where Σ∗\Sigma^{*}Σ∗ is obtained by truncating the sigular values of ∇f=UΣVT\nabla f=U \Sigma V^T∇f=UΣVT to be inside the range [k,K][k, K][k,K], i.e. σi∗=min⁡(max⁡(σi,k),K)\sigma_i^* = \min(\max(\sigma_i, k), K)σi∗​=min(max(σi​,k),K). This is indeed true. To see it, we write ∥∇f−Q∥F2=∥UΣVT−Q∥F2=∥Σ−UTQV∥F2\begin{aligned} \|\nabla f - Q\|_F^2 & = \|U \Sigma V^T - Q\|_F^2 \\ & = \| \Sigma - U^T Q V\|_F^2 \end{aligned}∥∇f−Q∥F2​​=∥UΣVT−Q∥F2​=∥Σ−UTQV∥F2​​ Let Q=SΣ′PTQ = S\Sigma' P^TQ=SΣ′PT be the sigular value decomposition of QQQ. The above expression is ∥Σ−UTSΣ′PTV∥F2=:∥Σ−U′TΣ′V′∥F2\| \Sigma - U^T S\Sigma' P^T V\|_F^2 =: \| \Sigma - U'^T\Sigma'V'\|_F^2∥Σ−UTSΣ′PTV∥F2​=:∥Σ−U′TΣ′V′∥F2​ which is equal to tr(ΣTΣ)−2tr(ΣTV′TΣ′U′)+tr(Σ′TΣ′)    (3)\text{tr}(\Sigma^T \Sigma) - 2\text{tr}(\Sigma^TV'^T\Sigma'U') + \text{tr}(\Sigma'^T\Sigma') \,\,\,\,(3)tr(ΣTΣ)−2tr(ΣTV′TΣ′U′)+tr(Σ′TΣ′)(3) Note that only the middle term has to do with the rotation matrices. The problem now turns into maximizing tr(ΣTU′TΣ′V′)\text{tr}(\Sigma^TU'^T\Sigma'V')tr(ΣTU′TΣ′V′) over orthonormal matrices U′,V′U', V'U′,V′. Suppose we have ordered the diagonal entries of Σ\SigmaΣ from large to small. Since they are all positive, we would like to maximize the diagonal entries of U′TΣ′V′U'^T\Sigma'V'U′TΣ′V′ and order them from large to small.

Proposition 3 Let U′,V′U',V'U′,V′ be orthonormal matrices, Σ′\Sigma'Σ′ be a matrix of zeros but non-negative on the diagonal. Suppose without loss of generality that the diagonal of Σ′\Sigma'Σ′ is ordered from large to small σ1′≥σ2′≥⋯\sigma_1' \geq \sigma_2' \geq \cdotsσ1′​≥σ2′​≥⋯. Then we have diag(U′TΣ′V′)≤diag(Σ′)\text{diag}(U'^T\Sigma' V') \leq \text{diag}(\Sigma')diag(U′TΣ′V′)≤diag(Σ′) where we use ≤\leq≤ as entry-wise comparison.

To prove this, observe that the kkk-th diagonal entry of U′TΣ′V′U'^T\Sigma' V'U′TΣ′V′ is uk′TΣ′vk′u_{k}'^T \Sigma' v_{k}'uk′T​Σ′vk′​ We state some simple lemmas following the above notation, and the proposition will follow immediately.

Lemma 4 If u,vu, vu,v are unit vectors, then uTΣ′vu^T \Sigma' vuTΣ′v is at most σ1′\sigma_1'σ1′​.

Lemma 5 If u,vu, vu,v are unit vectors such that uTΣ′v=σ1′u^T \Sigma' v = \sigma_1'uTΣ′v=σ1′​, then for any unit vectors u′,v′u', v'u′,v′ orthogonal to u,vu, vu,v repectively, u′TΣ′v′u'^T \Sigma' v'u′TΣ′v′ is at most σ2′\sigma_2'σ2′​.

These lemmas are in fact equivalent to the min-max characterization for singular values. Continue with the expression (3), we see when U′,V′U', V'U′,V′ are optimal, it is equal to tr(ΣTΣ)−2tr(ΣTΣ′)+tr(Σ′TΣ′)\text{tr}(\Sigma^T \Sigma) - 2\text{tr}(\Sigma^T\Sigma') + \text{tr}(\Sigma'^T\Sigma')tr(ΣTΣ)−2tr(ΣTΣ′)+tr(Σ′TΣ′) which is minimized when Σ′\Sigma'Σ′ is thresholded as described.
